points.en: Detail: choose a few concrete, sensory, telling details rather than a flood of description.
Economy: cut everything that does not serve, because clutter is the enemy of a story.
Tension: begin near the action, build to the turn and withhold the ending.
Point of view and single effect: decide whose eyes the hearer sees through, and aim every word at one dominant impression.
The story is told, not read: know it so well that notes are unnecessary, so the teller can look the people in the eye.
Pace it: hurry through the minor, slow at the turning point, and let silence work at the great moment.
Use the whole instrument of voice, face and body to carry the scene, and see the scene yourself so the hearers see it.
Feel it without performing it: genuine feeling moves people, while theatrics break the spell and the trust.
Marks: keep it short and moving, use concrete and specific detail, tell with warmth and conviction, and aim at the heart.
Technique stays honest when it serves the truth and the hearer and keeps the teller out of the way; once the congregation senses a performance, the trust breaks.
The story is a worthy vessel for the Word of God, and the preacher reaches the whole person, mind and heart.
Choose the form the truth requires; use Bible narratives, lives and parables as rich material, retold vividly and faithfully without adding to the text.
Illustrations are windows used honestly and with restraint, and the story is told well and true.
Over all, the story is a servant of the truth and of the hearer's meeting with God, never an end in itself.
The sermon studies Exodus 33 (Moses asks to see God's glory, the cleft of the rock) and finds one controlling image: the backside of God, the trail of glory where he has passed.
It contemporizes the image with a vivid modern picture and retells faithfully without adding to the text.
It lands one truth: we cannot see God's face now but can see where he has been, and that is enough to trust him with the road ahead.
Reading from a manuscript loses eye contact, spontaneity and life, so the hearer feels recited to.
Telling requires knowing the story so thoroughly that notes are unnecessary, so the teller can look at the people and pace it freely.
Single effect means a well-made story aims at one dominant impression, and every word bends toward it.
Economy serves it by cutting everything that does not contribute, so nothing dilutes or distracts from that one impression.
Delivery is a servant: skill in telling exists to carry the truth into the hearer's heart, not to display the teller or his gifts.
Good craft removes barriers between the truth and the hearer, while showy craft puts the teller in the way; the aim is the hearer's meeting with God.
The outline names a text and chooses a form (deductive, inductive or controlling story) that suits the text's truth.
It states a controlling image or the arc to be followed, aimed at one clear truth and faithful to the text.
It sketches how it will be told, such as point of view, key details, the turn and the close.
The thesis: the story, rightly and honestly used, is a worthy, God-honored vehicle for the Word, reaching the whole person and carrying truth to the heart.
The charge: study diligently, tell well and tell true, and keep the story always a servant of the truth and the hearer's meeting with God, never an end in itself.
Depends on the Spirit of God, so the preacher prepares fully and prays that he will breathe on the telling.
